title: Immune‐related aseptic meningitis diagnosed by Cube FLAIR on enhanced magnetic resonance imaging for a lung cancer patient administered atezolizumab: A case report
case_prompt: A 46-year-old man with a history of stage II squamous-cell lung cancer, treated surgically and with three prior lines of chemotherapy for recurrence, received his first dose of atezolizumab 10 days ago. He now presents with headache and fever. On admission, his Glasgow Coma Scale was E4V5M6. The following day he developed nausea, vomiting, and a decrease in consciousness to E4V3M5. A plain head CT scan showed no abnormalities. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 26 cells/μl (58% mononuclear, 42% polymorphonuclear), protein 451 mg/dl, glucose 68 mg/dl, and no bacteria. Empiric methylprednisolone (1000 mg/day) was started. On day 3, with further decline in consciousness to E4V2M5, gadolinium-enhanced brain MRI was performed. T1- and T2-weighted sequences were unremarkable, but a Gd-enhanced Cube FLAIR sequence demonstrated multiple nodular areas of contrast enhancement scattered over the surfaces of the cerebrum, cerebellum, and brainstem. By day 4, consciousness improved to E4V5M6. Repeat Gd-enhanced Cube FLAIR imaging on day 11 showed near-complete resolution of the nodules.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Leptomeningeal metastasis was considered given his cancer history, but imaging was unrevealing—“As intracranial lesion or leptomeningeal metastasis was suspected, he underwent plain head computed tomography (CT)… The head CT showed no abnormalities.”  
2. Bacterial meningitis was considered, but CSF culture was negative—“The cerebrospinal fluid contained no bacteria.”  
3. Encephalitis was a possibility, yet MRI showed no parenchymal inflammation—“There was no finding suggestive of encephalitis.”  
4. Paraneoplastic syndrome remained in the differential since autoantibody testing was not performed—“the paraneoplastic syndrome cannot be completely denied because the specific antibody was not measured.”  
5. Immune‐related aseptic meningitis rose in likelihood because of rapid clinical response to steroids and corresponding radiologic improvement—“An irAE was diagnosed based on the response to steroid therapy and the change of image findings.”
